doc.title: Randy Sandke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997

title: Race in jazz, marketing and Joshua Redman versus Chris Potter
summary: He wants music judged on its own terms, says New York clubs turn bebop into folklore, and compares attention given to Redman and Potter.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Is there any kind of racial thing happening in jazz right now that could be better?

Yeah. I think it definitely could be better. It’s not across the board, I think it’s just certain pockets of it. And I think in general it’s — the musicians have always been open minded They can hear, they can tell what’s going on. I mean I’ve had like for instance Bobby Watson, he once said to me, he said, “like I see so many white musicians being left behind, it’s not right,” and all that kind of stuff. And I mean they know what’s going on. And I don’t think — like white musicians I think feel very divided about it because they’re aware of the fact, of course forget like all that social discrimination that blacks have had to face for centuries, but you know like musically, the opportunities were very

limited for black players. I mean there’s a lot of great black players from the 20s who like in the 30s were out of the music business and doing other things. So they had it rough. But the part that bothers me is just people who should be a little bit objective. I’m just bothered any time the focus is not on the music. Music should be judged on its own terms, not on racial terms. And I think one of the things I see happening is that jazz and the way it’s being marketed, by promoters, producers, club owners and all that, it’s kind of turning into — like the New York club scene to me seems like it’s sort of turning to a folklore show. You know what I mean? I mean it’s like you go down to Mexico and you go into the place, and so for the tourist, and they have all the people wear their fancy clothes and bring out the guitars and do all this stuff. Well they’d probably not be caught dead in that if they weren’t getting paid to do that. And I mean I’m kind of stretching the point maybe a little. But I get the feeling that a lot of clubs in New York they feel like well a lot of money is coming from Japanese/ Europeans. They’re trying to recreate a scene of what they want New York to be. And that’s like having some young black guys play bebop, so that people can fantasize — oh man this is where Miles was and Trane — and that’s great, and that’s fine. But again that’s not a musical consideration. And there are young black guys who are fantastic. But there are also young white guys too. And I mean it’s like the older guys, I mean we’re another situation. But I mean just to take an example, and I would say now Joshua Redman, I think he’s one of the most talented of the younger musicians around today. I mean he knocks me out. He’s a great, great player. But so is Chris Potter. Chris Potter knocks me out too. Now Chris is working, he’s doing very well, he’s getting records out, but there’s no comparison between the kind of attention that Joshua gets, and also the freedom that Joshua gets to take his own group around. Because ultimately, see like it does ultimately have an effect on the music. Because here is one guy who is given the chance to develop his own thing. Now Chris can do that, but he’s got less of a chance. And it’s more like what I was talking about where maybe he’ll get a group together for a record date a week before and do it. But that’s different than having your own group to play at festival after festival for years. He’s going to be at a disadvantage. And I don’t want to say that it’s going to make his music less strong, but it makes it harder for him. And it’s just a reality of the situation now. And as I say that’s one of the reasons that I want to kind of focus my creative, original stuff more in the direction of classical music, contemporary classical music, because just frankly, I’m really tired of dealing with the whole thing. I just am a musician. Either you like my music or not. But just take it on those terms. And I just feel like jazz, it’s just like so many things have gotten in the way of that, for people like me. And as I say, I think the musicians themselves are pretty cool about it, although I am disturbed by some of the stuff at Lincoln Center going on. I think there is an agenda
